Hi! Ready for a quick game?
Level 1 starts now.
Try first: from memory, what is the lithosphere made of? Type your answer before reading on.
Here is the answer. The lithosphere is Earth's outer shell.
It is broken into a mosaic of rigid tectonic plates. A mosaic means many pieces fitted together, like a tile floor.
These plates float on the asthenosphere. That is the layer below.
It is ductile, meaning it can slowly flow.
Takeaway: plates are rigid; the layer under them flows.
Quick check: which layer can slowly flow? Type it.
Try first: can you name three forces that move the plates? Guess, then check.
The three forces are: mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push.
Mantle convection is slow churning of hot rock. Slab pull is a sinking plate edge pulling the rest.
Ridge push is new crust at a ridge pushing plates apart.
Picture it: a pot of very slow soup, churning round and round. The floating tiles on top drift as the soup moves.
Takeaway: three forces push and pull the plates.
Quick check: which force is a sinking plate edge pulling the rest? Type it.
Try first: how fast do plates move? Take a guess in units.
Plates move slowly. Speed is measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹).
That is about as fast as your fingernails grow.
Takeaway: plate speed is in centimetres per year.
Try first: what happens when two plates collide? Type your idea.
Plates meet at boundaries. There are three kinds.
Divergent -> plates pull apart -> normal faults, shallow quakes
Convergent -> plates collide -> thrust faults, deep to shallow
Transform -> plates slide past -> strike-slip, shallow to intermediate
Takeaway: three boundary types, three motion styles.
Quick check: at a transform boundary, what do plates do? Type it.
Try first: why do earthquakes cluster at boundaries? Write your best idea.
Here is the main reason. Plate edges are locked by friction.
Friction is the rubbing grip between surfaces.
Strain is stored stretching of rock. It builds until it exceeds rock strength.
Then it snaps: an earthquake.
Words: locked edge -> strain builds -> rock breaks -> quake.
Symbols: lock + strain ↑ -> strength limit -> SNAP.
Takeaway: locked edges store strain until rock snaps.
Watch out: the passage warns that quakes are not random. Do not say they happen anywhere.
They trace the pattern of plate motion.
Quick check from earlier: what unit measures plate speed? Type it.
Try first: can you name one other reason quakes cluster at boundaries? Guess first.
Three more reasons:
- Old faults concentrate slip.
- Cold, brittle lithosphere sits next to warm, ductile mantle. So squeezing focuses there.
- Curved plate margins force localized shear zones.
Takeaway: fault shape and rock contrast also focus quakes.
Said another way: earthquakes are not random. They trace the kinematic framework, the pattern of motion, where plates interact.

The lithosphere is the hard outer layer of Earth. It is broken into rigid plates.
Rigid means stiff and hard to bend.
Picture it like a cracked eggshell. Each crack piece is a plate.
The pieces float on a soft layer below.
That soft layer is the asthenosphere. It is ductile.
Ductile means soft and slow-flowing, like thick honey.

## Worked Examples: Plate Speeds and Earthquake Depths
Try first: before you read on, say what you already think about this.
Let's try a quick check first. From memory: which moves faster, the Pacific Plate or the Nazca Plate?
Hold that thought.
Plates move at set speeds. The Pacific Plate moves northwest at about 5 cm per year.
The Nazca Plate dives under South America at about 8 cm per year.
Fast plates mean more big quakes. These speeds help explain the many large earthquakes on the Ring of Fire.
Quick check: type the Nazca Plate speed. (Answer: 8 cm per year.)
Now depth. Shallow quakes are 10 km deep or less.
They happen at ridges and transform faults.
Deep quakes are 30 to 300 km down. They happen in the Wadati-Benioff zone, inside a sinking slab.
One subduction quake at 30 km depth gets energy from two sources: crust bending and the slab losing water.
Here is the depth map in one picture: Ridges / transform faults -> shallow (≤ 10 km) Subducting slab -> 30–300 km (Wadati-Benioff zone)
The seismic cycle has steps. Locked plates store strain for decades.
Slip releases it in seconds. Then stress shifts for months to years.
Last idea: a seismic gap is a segment that has not ruptured in a full cycle. Gaps are candidates for future large events.
Restated: the quiet spots may be the next to break.

## The Seismic Cycle at a Convergent Margin
Try first: before you read on, say what you already think about this.
Let's start with a quick check from memory. What happens first in an earthquake cycle?
Try to say it before you read on.
The cycle has steps. First is the interseismic step.
A locked zone holds strain. Strain is stored pushing force.
This lasts decades to centuries.
Next is the coseismic step. The fault slips fast.
Stored energy is released. This takes seconds to minutes.
Then the postseismic step. Afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation move stress around.
Afterslip is slow slip after the big quake. This lasts months to years.
There can also be a preseismic step. Warning signs may come first.
Foreshocks are small quakes before the big one. Slow slip is quiet fault movement.
Here is the cycle as a chain: interseismic (strain builds) ↓ coseismic (fast slip) ↓ postseismic (stress moves) preseismic signs may come before the big slip.
Plate speeds matter. The Pacific Plate moves about 5 cm per year.
The Nazca Plate goes under South America at about 8 cm per year. Fast speeds mean many big quakes in the Ring of Fire.
Depth matters too. Shallow quakes (10 km or less) happen at ridges and transform faults.
Deeper quakes (30 to 300 km) happen in the Wadati-Benioff zone of a sinking slab.
Seismic gap theory says this: a segment that has not ruptured in a full cycle may be a candidate for a future large event. Rupture means the fault breaks and slips.
GPS and InSAR measure plate speeds to refine coupling models. Coupling is how tightly plates are locked.
Restated once more: plates push for years, the fault locks and stores strain, then it slips fast, then stress settles after. Tomorrow, recall the four cycle steps in order.
